newsitem.title: UK: British budget -- Will Clarke keep one eye on EMU?.
newsitem.headline: British budget -- Will Clarke keep one eye on EMU?.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives would like nothing more than a vote-winning pre-election budget.

But Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is a different breed of political animal than many of the Tories and economists said next week's budget may have even bigger things in mind than the 1997 general election.

For one thing he is looking at the broad sweep of British economic trends, they said. Within that context, he is likely to go at least some way toward putting Britain on a firmer footing for European monetary union, if it ever decided to join.
"It will first and foremost be seen as something that was engineered in terms of prudence," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS in London.
But that carries with it the added political bonus of moving Britain closer to Maastricht criteria, and thus keeping the government's options open on a single currency, he said.
"The Chancellor would like to show we are more less on target to achieve the Maastricht target of three percent but I don't think it's a binding consideration," Garrard said.
Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley here, shared the view Clarke's own economic goals to some extent dovetailed with terms for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"He's doing a more difficult job than he would do going strictly on the Maastricht criteria. So really it (the EMU aspect) is veiled in a domestic need to meet the medium-term financial strategy."
Domestic economic priorities, and with them the EMU considerations, were thus set against the obvious political benefit of a loose fiscal position.
"Those two former points will win over and it (the budget) will be a compromise," Miller said.

Many analysts think EMU will only be a small factor at the back of Clarke's mind. They doubt he would even say the dreaded E-word in his speech for fear of upsetting the anti-EMU wing of his party. But that does not mean it will not be a factor.
"It (EMU) is one factor among several that's been causing me to argue he's not going to be fiscally irresponsible," said Joanne Collins, economist at Nomura International in London.
"He's pro-Europe and he wants to make sure that progress continues towards the Maastricht criteria," she said.

Among the key criteria, the treaty requires government budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP). Qualification on this ground, more than any of the other criteria, is determined by budget measures.
According to European Commission forecasts, Britain is one of only three countries along with Italy and Greece which will not bring its deficit to within the three percent goal in 1997.
The Commission in early November forecast Britain's deficit/GDP ratio would be 3.5 percent in 1997.

UBS has carried out analysis of Britain's public finances in terms of the European System of Integrated Accounts (ESA), by which the Maastricht terms are measured. One difficulty is that Britain is on a fiscal year through end-March while the EMU terms are based on calendar years.
But after adjusting for this, UBS earlier in the year made a forecast of a 4.1 percent deficit/GDP ratio for Britain in 1997 based on the strictest interpretation of the treaty terms.
Even after recent data showing a surprisingly large public sector debt repayment of 4.4 billion stg in October, Britain was on course for a deficit of around 3.8 percent, Garrard said.
Collins of Nomura said her calculations produced a four percent figure for 1997 based on a 25 billion stg public sector borrowing requirement.
But Garrard said Britain could still qualify. "All they have to show is that they are making a sustained effort to lower it on this basis in the direction of three percent," he said.
He said there was a 50/50 chance Clarke would refer to EMU in the speech, but he added either way the government's Red Book contained a table which put part of the budget into ESA terms.
The Red Book accompanies the budget and sets out spending plans.
Nonetheless, some analysts think EMU will hardly even figure in Clarke's priority list.

"To be honest, Kenneth Clarke is not enormously fussed about meeting the convergence criteria. The budget will be more a budget for domestic issues," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "If we were to meet Maastricht that's a bonus."
